questions.q: After fertilisation in a flowering plant, the ovary develops into a:
questions.explanation: The ovary wall develops into the fruit wall (pericarp), and the ovary becomes the fruit.

questions.q: After fertilisation, the ovule develops into a:
questions.explanation: The fertilised ovule matures into the seed, containing the embryo, stored food and a seed coat.

questions.q: The tender coconut water is an example of:
questions.explanation: Coconut water is free-nuclear endosperm, while the white kernel is the cellular endosperm.

questions.q: The remains of the persistent nucellus in a mature seed, as seen in black pepper and beet, is called:
questions.explanation: The residual, persistent nucellus is called perisperm.

questions.q: Pea seeds are non-albuminous because:
options: The endosperm is completely consumed by the developing embryo during seed development
Fertilisation does not occur in them
questions.explanation: In non-albuminous seeds such as pea and groundnut, no residual endosperm is left at maturity.

questions.q: In the embryo of grass family plants such as maize, the single cotyledon is represented by the:
questions.explanation: In monocots such as grasses the single cotyledon is called the scutellum, lying towards one side of the embryonal axis.

questions.q: Differentiate between albuminous and non-albuminous seeds with one example each.
questions.answer: Albuminous seeds retain a part of the endosperm because it is not completely used up during embryo development, as in wheat, maize and castor. Non-albuminous seeds have no residual endosperm, as it is totally consumed by the embryo, as in pea and groundnut.
questions.explanation: The difference depends on how much endosperm is left at seed maturity.

questions.q: Explain how seed formation gives flowering plants a survival advantage.
questions.answer: Seeds carry stored food that nourishes the young seedling until it can photosynthesise. A hard seed coat protects the embryo, and seeds can remain dormant until conditions are favourable. Seeds are also dispersed to new habitats, and they carry new genetic combinations because they result from sexual reproduction.
questions.explanation: These advantages help angiosperms to colonise diverse habitats.

questions.q: In the human male, sperms are stored and undergo maturation in the:
questions.explanation: The epididymis stores sperms, which become motile and mature there.

questions.q: The yellowish fluid secreted by the mammary glands in the first few days after delivery is called:
questions.explanation: Colostrum is rich in antibodies (IgA) and gives passive immunity to the newborn.

questions.q: The Sertoli cells of the seminiferous tubules:
options: Provide nutrition to the germ cells
questions.explanation: Sertoli cells nourish the germ cells and support spermatogenesis, whereas Leydig cells secrete androgens.

questions.q: Which of the following hormones is produced by the placenta?
questions.explanation: The placenta secretes hCG, human placental lactogen, oestrogens and progesterone.

questions.q: At the time of ovulation, the human secondary oocyte is arrested at which stage of meiosis?
questions.explanation: Meiosis II is arrested at metaphase II and completes only when a sperm enters the ovum.

questions.q: Menstrual cycles do not occur during pregnancy mainly because:
options: The ovaries stop producing eggs permanently
High levels of progesterone and oestrogen maintain the endometrium and inhibit ovulation
questions.explanation: The corpus luteum and placenta keep hormone levels high, so the endometrium is maintained and no ovulation or menstruation occurs.

questions.q: Describe the structure of a human sperm.
questions.answer: A sperm has a head, neck, middle piece and tail. The head has an elongated haploid nucleus covered by the acrosome with enzymes; the middle piece has many mitochondria that provide energy; the tail is a flagellum for motility.
keyPoints: Head with haploid nucleus and acrosome
questions.explanation: The plasma membrane envelops the whole sperm.

questions.q: Explain the process of parturition and the hormones involved.
questions.answer: Signals from the fully developed foetus and the placenta induce mild uterine contractions, called the foetal ejection reflex. This triggers the release of oxytocin from the maternal posterior pituitary, which acts on the uterine muscle to cause stronger contractions. A cycle of this positive feedback leads to the expulsion of the baby.
keyPoints: Foetal and placental signals start contractions
questions.explanation: Parturition is the process of delivery of the full-term foetus.

questions.q: Which of the following is a natural method of contraception?
questions.explanation: Periodic abstinence, withdrawal and lactational amenorrhoea are natural methods; they do not involve devices or drugs.

questions.q: Surgical sterilisation in the human male is called:
questions.explanation: In vasectomy a small part of the vas deferens is removed or tied, so sperms cannot be ejaculated.

questions.q: Medical termination of pregnancy is considered relatively safe during:
questions.explanation: MTPs are safest in the first trimester, that is, up to 12 weeks.

questions.q: In the gamete intra fallopian transfer (GIFT) technique:
options: An embryo is transferred into the uterus
An ovum from a donor is transferred into the fallopian tube of a female who cannot produce ova but can provide a suitable environment for fertilisation
A sperm is injected into an ovum
A zygote is transferred into the cervix
questions.explanation: GIFT transfers a donor ovum into the fallopian tube of a female unable to produce ova.

questions.q: Hormone-releasing IUDs such as LNG-20 prevent pregnancy by:
options: Making the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperms
Reducing sperm production in the testis
questions.explanation: Hormone-releasing IUDs make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperms.

questions.q: Copper ions released by a Cu-T prevent pregnancy because they:
options: Suppress sperm motility and the fertilising capacity of sperms
questions.explanation: Cu ions released by copper IUDs suppress sperm motility and fertilising capacity.

questions.q: Name two sexually transmitted infections and write two ways of preventing them.
questions.answer: Examples are gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes and hepatitis-B. Prevention includes avoiding sex with unknown partners or multiple partners, using condoms during coitus, and getting early detection and treatment.
keyPoints: Examples: gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, hepatitis-B
questions.explanation: Early detection and complete treatment reduce the spread of STIs.

questions.q: Differentiate between IUI and IVF.
questions.answer: In intra-uterine insemination (IUI), semen from the husband or a donor is artificially introduced into the uterus, and fertilisation happens inside the body. In IVF, the ovum and sperm are made to fuse in the laboratory and the embryo is transferred to the female reproductive tract.
keyPoints: IUI: semen placed in the uterus, fertilisation in the body
IVF: fertilisation outside in the laboratory
IVF embryo is transferred to fallopian tube or uterus
questions.explanation: Both are assisted reproductive technologies for infertile couples.

questions.q: Mendel selected how many pairs of contrasting characters in the garden pea for his experiments?
questions.explanation: Mendel studied seven pairs of contrasting traits such as seed shape, seed colour, plant height and flower colour.

questions.q: An individual having two identical alleles of a gene is called:
questions.explanation: Homozygous individuals have identical alleles, such as TT or tt.

questions.q: In a cross between two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt x Tt), what percentage of the offspring is expected to be dwarf?
questions.explanation: Tt x Tt gives 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, so one quarter are dwarf (tt).

questions.q: Human skin colour is an example of:
questions.explanation: Skin colour is controlled by several genes whose effects add up, which is polygenic inheritance.

questions.q: Two parents who are both carriers of the sickle-cell trait (HbA HbS) have a child. What is the probability that the child has sickle-cell anaemia (HbS HbS)?
questions.explanation: HbA HbS x HbA HbS gives 1 HbA HbA : 2 HbA HbS : 1 HbS HbS, so 25% are affected.

questions.q: In a dihybrid cross RrYy x RrYy for seed shape (R round, r wrinkled) and colour (Y yellow, y green), what fraction of F2 is round and green?
questions.explanation: Round green plants have genotype R_yy, with probability 3/4 x 1/4 = 3/16.

questions.q: State the chromosomal theory of inheritance.
questions.answer: Proposed by Sutton and Boveri, it states that genes are located on chromosomes. Chromosomes occur in pairs and segregate at gamete formation, and the behaviour of chromosomes during meiosis parallels that of Mendel's factors, so chromosomes are the carriers of hereditary units.
keyPoints: Chromosomes pair and segregate in meiosis
questions.explanation: Experimental verification was done by T. H. Morgan.

questions.q: Explain how a single base substitution leads to sickle-cell anaemia.
questions.answer: A point mutation changes the codon GAG to GUG in the gene for beta globin, so the sixth amino acid, glutamic acid, is replaced by valine. The mutant haemoglobin polymerises under low oxygen and makes the red blood cells sickle-shaped. It is an autosomal recessive disorder.
keyPoints: Glutamic acid replaced by valine in beta chain
questions.explanation: The disorder is an autosome-linked recessive trait.

questions.q: Which pair of nitrogenous bases in DNA are purines?
questions.explanation: Adenine and guanine are purines; cytosine, thymine and uracil are pyrimidines.

questions.q: In eukaryotes, the DNA in a nucleosome is wrapped around a core of:
questions.explanation: A nucleosome has about 200 base pairs of DNA wrapped around a histone octamer.

questions.q: The short fragments formed during discontinuous DNA synthesis on the lagging strand are called:
questions.explanation: Okazaki fragments are joined together by DNA ligase.

questions.q: Which are the three stop (termination) codons?
questions.explanation: UAA, UAG and UGA do not code for any amino acid and terminate translation.

questions.q: How many amino acids are incorporated when the mRNA 5'-AUG UUU GGC UAA-3' is translated?
questions.explanation: AUG, UUU and GGC code for three amino acids and UAA is a stop codon, which codes for none.

questions.q: The coding region of an mRNA has 303 nucleotides including the stop codon. How many amino acids are in the polypeptide?
questions.explanation: 303/3 = 101 codons; one is the stop codon, so 100 amino acids.

questions.q: What is transcription? Name the three regions of a transcription unit in bacteria.
questions.answer: Transcription is the process of copying genetic information from one strand of DNA into RNA, catalysed by RNA polymerase. A transcription unit has a promoter, the structural gene and a terminator.
keyPoints: Copying of a DNA strand into RNA
questions.explanation: The promoter is at the 5' end of the coding strand and the terminator at the 3' end.

questions.q: Why is DNA replication discontinuous on one of the two template strands?
questions.answer: DNA polymerase can synthesise DNA only in the 5' to 3' direction. On the template strand with 3' to 5' polarity the new strand is made continuously, but on the other template strand it must be made in short pieces in the opposite direction to fork movement, and these Okazaki fragments are joined by DNA ligase.
keyPoints: Lagging strand made in short fragments
questions.explanation: The strand made discontinuously is called the lagging strand.

questions.q: The study of fossils is called:
questions.explanation: Palaeontology is the study of fossils, which are remains of organisms of the past.

questions.q: Archaeopteryx is regarded as a connecting link between:
questions.explanation: Archaeopteryx had feathers and wings like birds, and teeth and a long tail like reptiles.

questions.q: Which of the following is a vestigial organ in humans?
questions.explanation: The vermiform appendix is reduced and functionless in humans, though it is well developed in herbivores.

questions.q: Which of the following was absent from the primitive atmosphere of the Earth?
questions.explanation: The early atmosphere had water vapour, methane, ammonia and hydrogen, but no free oxygen.

questions.q: The Oparin-Haldane hypothesis suggests that the first forms of life:
options: Arose by spontaneous generation from decaying matter
Arose from pre-existing non-living organic molecules through chemical evolution
questions.explanation: According to the theory, life originated from non-living organic molecules that formed in the primitive environment.

questions.q: A hominid with a brain capacity of about 900 cc, who probably ate meat, was:
questions.explanation: Homo erectus had a brain capacity of about 900 cc and probably ate meat.

questions.q: What are vestigial organs? Give two examples from the human body.
questions.answer: Vestigial organs are organs that are reduced in size and have lost their function, though they were functional in ancestors. Examples in humans are the vermiform appendix and the muscles that move the ear (or the nictitating membrane of the eye).
questions.explanation: They are evidence of evolution from ancestral forms.

questions.q: Compare the explanation of Lamarck and Darwin for the long neck of the giraffe.
questions.answer: Lamarck proposed that giraffes stretched their necks to reach leaves, and this acquired lengthening was passed to offspring (use and disuse). Darwin explained that giraffes naturally vary, and those with longer necks could feed better, survived and reproduced more, so the trait spread by natural selection.
keyPoints: Lamarck: use and disuse, inheritance of acquired characters
questions.explanation: Modern biology supports Darwin's explanation, as acquired characters are not inherited.

questions.q: Typhoid fever is usually spread through:
questions.explanation: Salmonella typhi enters the small intestine through contaminated food and water.

questions.q: Ringworm is caused by:
questions.explanation: Ringworm is a fungal disease caused by Microsporum, Trichophyton and Epidermophyton.

questions.q: The common cold is caused by:
questions.explanation: Rhinoviruses infect the nose and respiratory passage but not the lungs.

questions.q: Filariasis (elephantiasis) is caused by:
questions.explanation: Filarial worms of Wuchereria bancrofti and W. malayi cause chronic inflammation of the lymphatic vessels.

questions.q: Rheumatoid arthritis is called an autoimmune disease because:
options: It is caused by a virus
The body's immune system attacks its own cells
questions.explanation: In autoimmune disease the immune system fails to distinguish self from non-self and damages body cells.

questions.q: Which of the following is a physical carcinogen?
questions.explanation: X-rays and gamma rays are physical carcinogens, while tobacco smoke is chemical and oncogenic viruses are biological.

questions.q: Name the primary and secondary lymphoid organs of the human body.
questions.answer: The primary lymphoid organs are the bone marrow and thymus, where lymphocytes originate and mature. The secondary lymphoid organs are the spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches and MALT, where lymphocytes interact with antigens.
keyPoints: Secondary: spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches, MALT
questions.explanation: Lymphocytes mature in the primary organs.

questions.q: Explain why a person with AIDS usually dies of opportunistic infections and not of HIV directly.
questions.answer: HIV destroys the helper T cells, so the number of these cells declines progressively. The immune system becomes so weak that the person cannot fight common infections such as tuberculosis or fungal infections, and these infections cause death.
questions.explanation: The immune deficiency makes even weak pathogens dangerous.

questions.q: Which microbe is used for brewing beer and bread making?
questions.explanation: Saccharomyces cerevisiae, also called brewer's yeast, ferments sugars to ethanol and CO2.

questions.q: The nutritional quality of milk is improved on conversion to curd because it increases the amount of:
questions.explanation: Lactic acid bacteria increase the vitamin B12 content of milk.

questions.q: Streptokinase, used as a clot buster in patients with myocardial infarction, is produced by:
questions.explanation: Streptokinase is produced by the bacterium Streptococcus and modified by genetic engineering.

questions.q: Toddy, a traditional drink of some parts of southern India, is made by fermenting:
questions.explanation: Toddy is prepared by fermenting the sap of palms.

questions.q: What is the benefit of the fungal symbiont Glomus to the plants with which it associates?
options: Increased absorption of phosphorus from the soil
questions.explanation: Glomus forms mycorrhiza that absorbs phosphorus, and also gives resistance to root pathogens and salinity tolerance.

questions.q: Cattle dung is the common starting material in a biogas plant because it:
options: Already contains methanogens that are present in the rumen of cattle
questions.explanation: Methanogens present in the rumen of cattle help break down cellulose, so the dung is rich in these bacteria.

questions.q: Name two bioactive molecules obtained from microbes and state their uses.
questions.answer: Cyclosporin A, from the fungus Trichoderma polysporum, is an immunosuppressant used in organ transplant patients. Statins from Monascus purpureus lower blood cholesterol. Streptokinase breaks blood clots.
questions.explanation: Any two valid examples with uses are accepted.

questions.q: Describe what happens in the anaerobic sludge digester during sewage treatment and what is produced.
questions.answer: The activated sludge settled in the settling tank is pumped into large anaerobic digesters. Anaerobic bacteria digest the bacteria and fungi in the sludge, and they produce a mixture of gases (biogas) such as methane, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide, which can be used as energy.
keyPoints: Sludge is pumped to anaerobic digesters
Anaerobic bacteria digest the sludge microbes
Biogas of methane, H2S and CO2 is produced
questions.explanation: The effluent from the settling tank is released into water bodies.

questions.q: Restriction endonucleases are naturally found in:
questions.explanation: They are isolated from bacteria, where they protect the cell from invading viral DNA.

questions.q: Which technique is used to make multiple copies of a gene or DNA segment in vitro?
questions.explanation: PCR amplifies a target DNA sequence in vitro using primers and a thermostable DNA polymerase.

questions.q: Restriction exonucleases differ from endonucleases in that:
options: Exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends of DNA, while endonucleases cut at specific positions within DNA
Endonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends of DNA
questions.explanation: Exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends, whereas restriction endonucleases cut at specific internal sites.

questions.q: A selectable marker in a cloning vector helps to:
options: Identify and eliminate non-transformants and allow selective growth of transformants
Cut the DNA at specific sites
questions.explanation: Genes for antibiotic resistance are used as selectable markers to identify transformants.

questions.q: Agrobacterium tumefaciens is used for gene transfer into dicot plants because:
options: Its plasmid contains the lacZ gene
Its Ti plasmid can be disarmed and used to deliver T-DNA carrying a gene of interest into plant cells
It is a virus that infects plants
questions.explanation: Agrobacterium naturally transfers T-DNA into plant cells, so it is used as a natural genetic engineer.

questions.q: In the biolistics (gene gun) method, plant cells are bombarded with:
options: Microscopic particles of gold or tungsten coated with DNA
questions.explanation: High-velocity DNA-coated microparticles of gold or tungsten are shot into plant cells.

questions.q: What is a palindromic nucleotide sequence? Give an example.
questions.answer: It is a sequence of base pairs that reads the same on the two strands when read in the same 5' to 3' direction, such as 5'-GAATTC-3' and 3'-CTTAAG-5'. Restriction enzymes cut DNA at such sequences.
keyPoints: Same sequence on both strands read 5' to 3'
questions.explanation: Restriction enzymes recognise palindromic sites.

questions.q: Outline the steps used to isolate pure DNA from bacterial cells.
questions.answer: The cells are broken open with lysozyme (cellulase for plant cells and chitinase for fungi). RNA is removed by ribonuclease and proteins by protease. Chilled ethanol is then added, and the DNA precipitates as fine threads that can be spooled out.
keyPoints: Lysis of cell wall with enzyme
Removal of RNA and proteins by ribonuclease and protease
Precipitation of DNA with chilled ethanol
questions.explanation: Purified DNA is then cut by restriction enzymes.

questions.q: Bt cotton is resistant to:
options: Certain insect pests such as bollworms
questions.explanation: Bt cotton makes Bt toxin, which kills the larvae of bollworms.

questions.q: Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency is a condition in which:
options: The enzyme adenosine deaminase is missing, causing immune dysfunction
questions.explanation: ADA deficiency affects the immune system, and was the first disease treated with gene therapy.

questions.q: Which technique is used to detect HIV in suspected AIDS patients at an early stage, before symptoms appear?
questions.explanation: PCR can amplify the small amount of HIV nucleic acid so that it can be detected early.

questions.q: In India, the body that decides on the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM organisms for public services is:
questions.explanation: The Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC) makes decisions about GM research and its safety.

questions.q: Transgenic animals have been used to produce alpha-1-antitrypsin, a protein used to treat:
questions.explanation: Alpha-1-antitrypsin is used to treat emphysema.

questions.q: The bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis is not killed by its own Bt toxin because:
options: The toxin is not made by it
The toxin is made as an inactive protoxin that is activated only in the alkaline gut of the insect
questions.explanation: The protoxin is converted to active toxin by the alkaline pH in the insect gut, which solubilises the crystals.

questions.q: How does the Bt toxin kill an insect larva?
questions.answer: The inactive protoxin crystals are ingested by the larva and are solubilised in the alkaline pH of its gut. The activated toxin binds to the epithelial cells of the midgut and creates pores, causing the cells to swell and lyse, and the larva dies.
keyPoints: Pores form in gut epithelium, cells lyse, larva dies
questions.explanation: The toxin is harmless to humans because the human gut is not alkaline.

questions.q: Explain the mechanism of RNA interference (RNAi).
questions.answer: RNAi is a cellular defence in all eukaryotes in which double-stranded RNA (from sources like viruses or transposons) is processed, and the resulting RNA binds to a specific complementary mRNA and silences it, so it is not translated. In biotechnology, this is used to silence genes of pests.
keyPoints: mRNA is silenced and not translated
questions.explanation: It is used to make nematode-resistant tobacco plants.

questions.q: A group of individuals of the same species living in a given geographical area is called a:
questions.explanation: A population consists of individuals of one species in a specific area at a given time.

questions.q: Lichens represent a mutualistic association between:
options: A fungus and an alga or cyanobacterium
questions.explanation: The fungus absorbs nutrients and the photosynthetic partner provides food.

questions.q: The Abingdon tortoise in the Galapagos Islands became extinct within a decade of goats being introduced there, because:
options: Goats were more efficient browsers and out-competed the tortoises for food
questions.explanation: The goats' greater browsing efficiency eliminated the tortoise, an example of interspecific competition.

questions.q: Which of the following is a typical adaptation of parasites?
options: A large body with powerful limbs
questions.explanation: Parasites often lose unnecessary sense organs and develop adhesive organs, suckers and high reproductive capacity.

questions.q: A bacterial culture begins with 500 cells and the population doubles every 20 minutes. Ideally, how many cells will be present after 1 hour?
questions.explanation: One hour is three doublings: 500 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 4000.

questions.q: Small animals such as shrews and hummingbirds are rarely found in polar regions because they:
options: Have a large surface area relative to volume, so they lose heat quickly and need a high metabolic cost to keep warm
questions.explanation: Small animals lose body heat fast, so they would have to spend much energy to stay warm in cold regions.

questions.q: Name four important abiotic factors that influence organisms.
questions.answer: The important abiotic factors are temperature, water, light and soil. Temperature affects enzyme activity, water is essential for life, light affects photosynthesis and many behaviours, and soil composition affects the vegetation and animals in a place.
questions.explanation: Abiotic factors shape the distribution of organisms.

questions.q: What is competitive release? Describe an example.
questions.answer: Competitive release is the sudden expansion of the distributional range of a species when its competitor is removed. In Connell's experiment on the rocky coast of Scotland, the barnacle Chthamalus expanded its range when its competitor Balanus was removed.
keyPoints: Range of a species expands when its competitor is removed
questions.explanation: It shows that competition restricts the realised niche of a species.

questions.q: An aquarium or a crop field is an example of a:
questions.explanation: Crop fields and aquaria are man-made ecosystems.

questions.q: Primary productivity is defined as:
options: The total biomass of consumers only
The amount of biomass or organic matter produced per unit area over a time period by plants during photosynthesis
questions.explanation: It is expressed in terms of weight (g/m2) or energy (kcal/m2).

questions.q: Humus is:
options: A dark-coloured, amorphous substance resistant to microbial action, acting as a reservoir of nutrients
Fresh leaf litter on the soil
questions.explanation: Humus is highly resistant to microbial action and undergoes decomposition at an extremely slow rate.

questions.q: The release of inorganic nutrients from humus by the action of microbes is called:
questions.explanation: Humus is degraded by microbes and inorganic nutrients are released, which is mineralisation.

questions.q: Decomposition of detritus will be slowest in which situation?
options: Detritus rich in nitrogen and sugars
Detritus rich in lignin and chitin in cold, dry conditions
questions.explanation: Lignin and chitin decompose slowly, and low temperature and dryness inhibit microbial activity.

questions.q: In hydrarch succession in a pond, the pioneer community consists of:
questions.explanation: Small phytoplankton are the pioneers, followed by submerged, floating, reed-swamp and marsh stages and finally forest.

questions.q: What is productivity? Differentiate between gross and net primary productivity.
questions.answer: Productivity is the rate of biomass production. Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis. Net primary productivity (NPP) is GPP minus the respiration losses, and it is the biomass available to consumers.
keyPoints: Productivity is the rate of biomass production
questions.explanation: NPP is the food available for heterotrophs.

questions.q: Describe the steps of decomposition of detritus.
questions.answer: Detritivores break the detritus into smaller particles in fragmentation. Water-soluble inorganic nutrients move down the soil by leaching. Bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade the detritus into simpler substances in catabolism. Humification forms humus, and mineralisation finally releases inorganic nutrients.
questions.explanation: These steps occur simultaneously in the soil.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of ex situ conservation?
questions.explanation: Botanical gardens, zoos and seed banks conserve species outside their natural habitat.

questions.q: The Earth Summit of 1992, which called upon nations to take appropriate measures for biodiversity conservation, was held at:
questions.explanation: The Convention on Biological Diversity came out of the Earth Summit held in Rio de Janeiro.

questions.q: Species that are found only in a particular region and nowhere else are called:
questions.explanation: Endemic species are restricted to one region; hotspots have a high level of endemism.

questions.q: Biodiversity hotspots are regions with:
options: High species richness, high endemism and accelerated habitat loss
questions.explanation: Hotspots are rich in species and endemics, and are under threat of habitat loss.

questions.q: In species-area relationship studies of very large areas such as entire continents, the slope (Z) of the line is:
options: 0.1-0.2, the same as for smaller areas
0.6-1.2, much steeper than for smaller areas
questions.explanation: Z is 0.1-0.2 for most regions, but it is 0.6-1.2 when analysing very large areas.

questions.q: The extinction of the passenger pigeon and Steller's sea cow is an example of loss of biodiversity due to:
questions.explanation: Both were driven to extinction by excessive hunting or harvesting.

questions.q: Differentiate between in situ and ex situ conservation with examples.
questions.answer: In situ conservation protects species in their natural habitat, for example national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves and sacred groves. Ex situ conservation protects threatened species outside their habitat, for example zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks and cryopreservation of gametes.
keyPoints: In situ: natural habitat (national parks, sanctuaries)
Ex situ: outside habitat (zoos, seed banks)
questions.explanation: In situ conservation is considered the best method.

questions.q: How does habitat fragmentation threaten animals such as large mammals and migratory birds?
questions.answer: Fragmentation breaks large habitats into small patches. Mammals and birds that need large territories cannot survive in small patches, and migratory species lose their routes. Isolated populations also decline in size, which can lead to local extinction.
keyPoints: Large habitats break into small patches
Animals needing large territories or migrating are affected
Small isolated populations are prone to extinction
questions.explanation: Habitat loss and fragmentation is the major cause of biodiversity loss.
